Conﬁdential manuscript submitted to Space Weather
A variational approach to Data Assimilation in the
Solar Wind
Matthew Lang 1, Mathew J. Owens 2
1Le Laboratoire des Sciences du Climat et de l’Environnement, CEA-CNRS-UVSQ, 91191 Gif Sur Yvette,
France
2Department of Meteorology, University of Reading, Reading, Berkshire, UK
Key Points:
• This paper develops a variational data assimilation (DA) method and applies it
to a simple solar wind propagation model.
• Such a DA scheme enables the inner boundary of the solar wind model to be
updated using observations in near-Earth space.
• Experiments performed with both synthetic and STEREO observations show
that the DA method is able to reduce errors in the solar wind speeds.
Corresponding author: Matthew Lang, matthew.lang@lsce.ipsl.fr
–1–
arXiv:1806.07306v3  [physics.space-ph]  2 Oct 2018

Conﬁdential manuscript submitted to Space Weather
Abstract
Variational Data Assimilation (DA) has enabled huge improvements in the skill of
operational weather forecasting. In this study, we use a simple solar-wind propagation
model to develop the ﬁrst solar-wind variational DA scheme. This scheme enables
solar-wind observations far from the Sun, such as at 1 AU, to update and improve
the inner boundary conditions of the solar wind model (at 30 solar radii). In this
way, observational information can be used to improve estimates of the near-Earth
solar wind, even when the observations are not directly downstream of the Earth. Us-
ing controlled experiments with synthetic observations we demonstrate this method’s
potential to improve solar wind forecasts, though the best results are achieved in con-
junction with accurate initial estimates of the solar wind. The variational DA scheme

Implications for an ideal-MHD solver **[derived]**:
- An adiabatic γ = 5/3 plasma with n ∝ R^−2 gives T ∝ R^−1.33. γ = 1.5 gives R^−1.0. Observed proton exponents at 0.3–1 AU are −0.58 (slow) to −0.9 (fast), so the observed effective proton polytropic index is ≈ 1.3–1.46 (Totten: 1.46 ± 0.16; Dakeyo γ_p 1.35–1.59).
- Expect your γ = 5/3 runs to under-predict 1 AU T_p unless the boundary T is raised; γ = 1.5 is closer.
- Note: Hofmeister et al. (2026) normalize T by (r/r₀)^{4/3} (the γ = 5/3 adiabatic scaling).

Parker-spiral angle at 1 AU **[derived]**: tan ψ = Ω r cos(lat)/v, with Ω = 2.865×10⁻⁶ rad/s (sidereal 25.38 d), so Ω·(1 AU) = 428.6 km/s. That gives ψ = 50.8° (350 km/s), 47.0° (400), 40.6° (500), 29.7° (750).
- Hellinger 2013 §3.2 quotes "about 50°" for 350 km/s **[text]**.
- Perrone 2019 fits give atan(\|B_t\|/\|B_r\|) ≈ 40° at 1 AU for coronal-hole fast wind **[derived]**.
- An observed ψ distribution (Borovsky 2010; Thomas & Smith 1980) was not read **[UNVERIFIED]**.

  - Means: 6.16 nT, 418 km/s, 6.48 cm⁻³, 1.13×10⁵ K.
  - The speed distribution is fitted by two lognormals peaking at 368 and 489 km/s.
- Le Chat et al. 2012 Table 1 **[text]**: slow wind (400 km/s) n = 4.7 cm⁻³, T_p = 0.8×10⁵ K; fast wind (750 km/s) n = 1.4 cm⁻³, T_p = 2.8×10⁵ K. Le Chat uses T_p ≈ 0.5 V² (K, with V in km/s).
- Jian et al. 2019 Table 2 **[text]**, ambient-wind means, Cycle 23 OMNI vs Cycle 24 STEREO: B 6.8 vs 5.26 nT, V 442 vs 401 km/s, P_dyn 2.27 vs 1.52 nPa.

### 2.2 n–v anticorrelation and flux invariance

- **Energy flux W = ρV(V²/2 + GM_s/R_s)** (Le Chat, Issautier & Meyer-Vernet 2012, Sol. Phys., arXiv:1203.1316) **[text]**:
  - §3.1, protons only: ⟨W⟩ at 1 AU = (1.5 ± 0.4)×10⁻³ W m⁻² (Helios 1.4, Ulysses 1.7, Wind 1.3, all ×10⁻³).
  - §3.3, with alphas: ⟨W⟩ = (1.7 ± 0.4)×10⁻³ W m⁻², i.e., 79 W m⁻² at 1 R_s.
  - Independent of speed and latitude within 10%.
  - Most probable value (Wind 1994–2011): 8.5×10⁻⁴ W m⁻².
  - Eq. 3: ρ ≈ 1.7×10⁻¹² [V(V² + 3.81×10⁵)]⁻¹, ρ in kg m⁻³, V in km/s; valid up to 700 km/s.
  - Fig. 4: solar-minimum (2007–2009) mean P_dyn 1.57 nPa (Wind) and 1.70 nPa (Ulysses).
- **[derived]** from Le Chat Eq. 3: dln n/dln V = −1.6 at 400 km/s and −2.2 at 750 km/s. ρV² = 1.28 nPa at 400 and 1.35 nPa at 750 km/s. The momentum flux is nearly speed-independent, which supports the n v² = const boundary rule used by ENLIL and EUHFORIA.
- **PSP:** W normalized to 1 R_s = 69.4 (≈ 70 ± 14) W m⁻²; W ∝ r^−1.92 (Liu et al. 2021, A&A, arXiv:2101.03121) **[text]**.
- **Boundary rules in other codes:**
  - MS-FLUKSS (Hegde et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.22386, §II.4) **[text]**: N V_R² = N_min V_fast² and N T = N_min T_max, with N_min = 200 cm⁻³, T_max = 2 MK, V_fast = 700 km/s.
  - ENLIL: see Section 1, Recipe D. A CCMC 2012 deck (search snippet only) gives fast stream 200 cm⁻³ and 1.0 MK at 0.1 AU, and a 2007 deck 300 cm⁻³ and 1 MK **[UNVERIFIED]**.
- Wang (2010, ApJL 715, L121) and McGregor et al. (2011, JGR, doi:10.1029/2010JA016006): only abstracts or secondary descriptions found **[UNVERIFIED]**.
  - Wang 2010: mass flux about constant at 1 AU.
  - McGregor 2011 (WSA-ENLIL): most speed change happens within a few tenths of an AU, the largest for 400–500 km/s wind.

Derived 1 → 1.5 AU scalings of SIR medians (Geyer 2021) **[derived]**: n_max ∝ r^−2.0, B_max ∝ r^−1.6, Pt_max ∝ r^−3.2.
- Peak density and field fall roughly like the ambient wind, while the magnetic compression ratio grows ×1.18 (Henderson 2025).
- The shock fraction rises from ≈ 13–33% at 1 AU to ≈ 36–56% at 1.5 AU and ≈ 60% over 1–3 AU.
- Model-validation implication: an MHD model run 0.1 → 2.5 AU should show compression ratios growing with r and most SIR shocks forming between ~1 and ~3 AU. Recall that MHD models tend to under-produce SIR compression (Hofmeister 2026 §2; Jian 2015 §4).

Not verified by either of us: Ebert et al. 2009 (Ulysses slow/fast tables), Schwenn (1990) acceleration numbers, Maksimovic et al. 2020 class speeds, the Gosling & Pizzo (1999) shock-formation criteria, and Wang (2010)."
